e-e810053047.text: TIER 3. What the report establishes: General Norlain, then director of the IHEDN, writes that 'when General Letty visited me in March 1995 at my office at IHEDN to explain to me his project for creating a new fact-finding committee on UFOs, I assured him of my interest and referred him to the management of the IHEDN Auditors Association'. e-fd1c239a20.label: French national UAP office, CNES Toulouse
e-fd1c239a20.text: CNES describes GEIPAN as 'the French UAP research and information group created by CNES in 1977', based in Toulouse, overseen by COPEIPAN - a steering committee of gendarmerie, police, air and space force and academic representatives - with status 'In operation' and an indefinite lifetime.

claimed.text: COMETA's report concludes that the studies show the almost certain physical reality of completely unknown flying objects apparently operated by intelligent beings, that secret craft of earthly origin can explain only a minority of cases, and that the single hypothesis that accounts for the facts is that of extraterrestrial visitors.

Letty's foreword argues that well-documented sightings by credible witnesses force consideration of every hypothesis, the extraterrestrial one in particular. The report puts its category D cases at 4 to 5% and says that with so many such cases the file can no longer be classed as needing no action.

COMETA says about a hundred GEPAN/SEPRA investigations included several that showed the physical presence of an unknown phenomenon, naming Trans-en-Provence and Amaranth, and that of twelve French aeronautical cases only three or four fall into category D.

Its recommendations are to boost SEPRA's resources and foreign standing, create a unit at the highest level of the state to work with it, prepare for a spectacular manifestation, warn defence communication services about disinformation, and make diplomatic approaches urging the United States to collaborate.

COMETA's members, as printed in the report, include retired generals, an admiral, a weapons engineer general, a Police Nationale chief and a research director at the national aerospace research office ONERA.

The same Westrum summary, held in the NSA's collection, says GEPAN's 1978 report found in 10 of 11 cases that witnesses had seen a material phenomenon that could not be explained as natural or as a human device, and that behind the phenomenon there was a flying machine whose means of lift and propulsion were beyond present knowledge; it praises the care of the investigations against the Condon Report.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's chief of staff, Olivier Schrameck, said Jospin read and annotated the report to mark his interest; the government made no official response. One account says Velasco handed the report to Jospin in person.
The US Department of War's 2026 release is reported to cite the COMETA report in its section on investigations outside the United States, in connection with the 1995 Bariloche airliner case.

contested.text: The state office and the private report read the numbers differently: COMETA put its category D at 4 to 5% in 1999, while GEIPAN's 2026 figure is 3.1 to 3.2%, and GEIPAN itself disclaims being a UFO or extraterrestrial research group at all.
The records differ on GEIPAN's size: its own description gives two full-time CNES staff, while the Sky Canada report gives three full-time employees and over 20 trained volunteers.

The COMETA report does not itself record delivery to the head of government; it says only that its authors thought the President and Prime Minister should be informed, and it never names Paris in connection with the association.

COMETA was a private association under the 1901 law, operating informally from 1996, registered in 1999 and dormant from about 2006, not a government body; its report first appeared as a special issue of the magazine VSD.

When French analysts, through GEIPAN, worked the 2014 Chilean Navy infrared footage, they proposed an airliner venting wastewater, which the Chilean office rejected; independent analysts later matched the footage to scheduled flights.

lead.text: France has studied unidentified aerospace phenomena inside its national space agency, CNES, since 1977: first as GEPAN, then SEPRA from 1988, and since 2005 as GEIPAN, which publishes its case files. Separately, in 1999 a private group of retired generals and defence auditors, COMETA, published a report arguing for the extraterrestrial hypothesis.

record.text: GEIPAN is a CNES unit at Toulouse, listed by CNES as in operation for an indefinite lifetime, steered by a committee of representatives of the Gendarmerie, civil aviation, meteorology, the Air Force, scientific research and CNES, and supported by about thirty volunteer experts and field investigators.

GEIPAN classifies each case by the consistency of the testimony and its residual strangeness, into A (perfectly identified), B (probably identified), C (unidentified for lack of data) and D (unidentified after investigation); its statistics dated 11 August 2026 cover 3,381 cases, of which 106, 3.1%, are class D.

GEIPAN says it receives more than 1,000 contacts a year, of which about 150 to 200 lead to an investigation published on its site with the witnesses kept anonymous; its team is two full-time CNES staff, funded from CNES's general subsidy rather than a dedicated budget.

GEIPAN's own FAQ states that it is a technical department of CNES, not a security or alert service, and not a research group on UFOs or extraterrestrial life, working only from recognised scientific knowledge.

A contemporaneous English-language summary by Ron Westrum of GEPAN's 1978 report, held in the NSA's declassified UFO collection, notes that the original report was limited to 120 or 140 copies and was secret, and that GEPAN was alerted to cases by Gendarmerie teletype.
GEPAN's investigation of the Trans-en-Provence physical-trace case of 8 January 1981 was published as Note Technique no. 16 and is still hosted on the GEIPAN site.

In his COMETA preface Norlain records that the IHEDN auditors' first report had favoured creating within CNES the only civilian government agency in the world dedicated to UFOs, and asks that COMETA's recommendations be examined and implemented; Lebeau's foreword is titled as stripping the phenomenon of its irrational layer.
COMETA's report adopts Hynek's Blue Book-era classification for its strangest cases and carries an appendix titled The Roswell Affair - Disinformation.
The Sky Canada Project held GEIPAN up as a model, recording that only 3.2% of its 3,188 cases by 2025 remained unidentified after investigation, and recommended that Canada partner with it.

summary.text: A 1976 committee of the defence studies institute IHEDN, chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie, opened the file, and its recommendations were followed in creating GEPAN inside CNES in 1977 under Claude Poher.

GEPAN became SEPRA in 1988, the permanent CNES unit that also monitored orbital debris and risk objects; after an audit ordered in 2001, CNES replaced SEPRA with GEIPAN in 2005, with a recommendation to inform the public with full transparency, and began publishing the archives in 2007.

COMETA, led by General Denis Letty and sponsored through the IHEDN auditors' association after Letty went to General Bernard Norlain in 1995, produced its report in July 1999 with a foreword by the former CNES chairman Andre Lebeau and contributions from SEPRA's head, Jean-Jacques Velasco.

On the board's reading, France and Britain gave opposite answers to the same problem: France placed the file in a civil science agency with a public archive, which still runs, while Britain kept it in a defence secretariat and closed it.
